1.quote_or_event: “Through these fifty-two letters, the three worlds and all things are described. These letters shall perish; they cannot describe the Imperishable Lord.”
1.explanation: Kabir opens his acrostic on the alphabet by saying every letter points beyond itself to the One who precedes all speech; the same composition goes on, “I know only the One, the Universal Creator, the Primal Being.” The Guru Granth Sahib itself begins with the numeral 1 in Ik Onkar, putting the One before every word that follows.
1.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Kabir uses the alphabet to say that God is first and is the source of everything the letters go on to describe.
1.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 340, Raag Gauri Poorbi, Bavan Akhri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1._accuracy_note: Verbatim on srigranth.org; the alphabet-and-the-Primal-One device closely matches the Kural, though Kabir stresses that letters cannot capture God where Valluvar stresses priority.

2.quote_or_event: “You may read and read loads of books; you may read and study vast multitudes of books... O Nanak! Only one thing is of any account: everything else is useless babbling and idle talk in ego.”
2.explanation: Guru Nanak piles up images of endless study (cartloads, boatloads, a lifetime of reading) and then says that only one thing counts, the Name of God. Without that, learning is just ego talking.
2.tie_back: Same verdict as the Kural: learning that never bows to the source of wisdom is worth nothing.
2.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
2._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org (ellipsis marks the omitted middle lines); a near one-to-one match on the uselessness of learning without devotion.

3.quote_or_event: “I am a sacrifice to those who remain lovingly attached to the Lord’s Feet. They are like the lotus which remains detached, floating upon the water. They are peaceful and beautiful forever.”
3.explanation: This pauri praises those who hold fast to the Lord’s feet. It compares them to a lotus that floats on water without being soaked, and says they stay peaceful and beautiful forever.
3.tie_back: Clinging to the divine feet, with a flower image attached, brings a lasting and settled flourishing, which is what the Kural promises.
3.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1281, Raag Malar, Vaar Malar, Pauri 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
3._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the feet and flower imagery and the promise of lasting peace match well, though in Gurbani the lotus stands for the devotee, not for God's footing, and the reward is spiritual rather than long earthly life.

4.quote_or_event: “One Universal Creator God. The Name Is Truth. Creative Being Personified. No Fear. No Hatred. Image Of The Undying, Beyond Birth, Self-Existent. By Guru’s Grace ~”
4.explanation: The Mool Mantar, the opening creed of the Guru Granth Sahib, defines God as nirbhau (without fear) and nirvair (without hatred or enmity). God is beyond the pulls of attraction and aversion that drive human beings.
4.tie_back: The Kural's God is beyond craving and aversion. The Sikh creed likewise names freedom from fear and hatred as defining marks of the One in whom devotees take refuge.
4.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Mool Mantar (opening of Japji Sahib), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
4._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; nirvair corresponds well to freedom from aversion, but the creed does not itself state the Kural's second claim that refuge in such a God ends suffering.

5.quote_or_event: “On the banks of sacred rivers, the mind is not appeased. People remain entangled in good and bad deeds. Sin and virtue are both the same.”
5.explanation: Kabir says people stay tangled up in both their good and their bad deeds, and that as bonds the two are the same. Release does not come from piling up merit. It comes from the treasure already within, the Name.
5.tie_back: This is the Kural's own point: both kinds of karma bind, and only true knowledge of God lifts a person out of them.
5.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 325, Raag Gauri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
5._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a strong conceptual match on good and bad deeds equally binding, though Kabir does not use the Kural's darkness/ignorance image.

6.quote_or_event: “In the one village of the body, live the five thieves; they have been warned, but they still go out stealing. One who keeps his assets safe from the three modes and the ten passions, O Nanak! Attains liberation and emancipation.”
6.explanation: Sikh teaching names five thieves living in the body: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego. Whoever guards against them and against the restless passions reaches liberation.
6.tie_back: The Kural ties a flourishing life to mastering the five senses. Guru Nanak ties liberation to holding the body's five inner thieves in check.
6.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 503, Raag Gujri, Ashtpadi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
6._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong thematic fit on mastering a fivefold inner force, but the Sikh five thieves are vices rather than the five sense faculties, and the Kural speaks of God's mastery while Nanak speaks of the seeker's.

7.quote_or_event: “That Primal Being is Immaculate and Pure. The Lord, the Primal Being, is Immaculate and Pure. The Lord is Inaccessible, Unreachable and unrivaled... Meditate on the Lord, O Saints; He is the Dispeller of all sorrow.”
7.explanation: Guru Ram Das's So Purakh, sung daily in the evening prayer Rehras, calls the Lord unrivaled and the remover of all sorrow. It tells the saints to meditate on Him.
7.tie_back: The Kural joins the same two ideas: anxiety is lifted only by holding to the One who has no equal.
7.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, Raag Asa, So Purakh, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
7._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted lines); both elements of the Kural, incomparability and relief from sorrow, appear in the same hymn.

8.quote_or_event: “The soul is enlightened, and the intellect is exalted, meditating on the Lord, the ocean of excellence.”
8.explanation: Guru Amar Das calls the Lord an ocean of excellence (gun, virtue). Elsewhere Gurbani repeatedly calls worldly life a terrifying world-ocean that only the Name can carry one across.
8.tie_back: The Kural sets an ocean of virtue against the ocean of worldly existence. Gurbani uses the same pair of oceans, though this verse names only the first.
8.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 516, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
8._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; 'ocean of excellence' matches the Kural's 'ocean of virtue', but the crossing of the world-ocean is not in this verse and is supplied from Gurbani's wider imagery (see Ang 1009).

9.quote_or_event: “The head which does not bow to the Lord - chop off and remove that head. That head which does not bow to the Lord - what is to be done with that head? Put it in the fireplace, instead of firewood.”
9.explanation: Sheikh Farid, the Sufi saint whose verses the Gurus included in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that a head which will not bow to God has lost its purpose. It is fit only to be burned as firewood.
9.tie_back: Both the Kural and Farid judge an unbowed head useless, because it fails at the one thing it exists for.
9.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Saloks 71-72 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
9._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; near one-to-one on the useless unbowed head, though Farid's simile is firewood where the Kural's is a dead sense-organ. Farid's verses are canonical scripture in Sikhism.

10.quote_or_event: “There are no oars, nor any boatmen, to cross over the terrifying world-ocean... The True Name of the True Lord is there; it carries them across the terrifying world-ocean.”
10.explanation: Guru Nanak says human means cannot cross the world-ocean; only the True Name carries a person over. In the same hymn he says the Gurmukhs reach the far shore and their comings and goings in rebirth come to an end.
10.tie_back: Same picture as the Kural: only through God can one cross the great ocean of repeated births.
10.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1009, Raag Maru, Ashtpadi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
10._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks one omitted line); a near one-to-one match on crossing the ocean of births through God alone.
